source.title: Characterizing the Generalization Error of Random Feature Regression with Arbitrary Data-Augmentation
source.authors: L. Morisset; Alain Durmus; Adrien Hardy

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure content is garbled in the supplied text, so numerical values from those plots cannot be recovered.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures test risk while varying the sample-to-feature aspect ratio in random-feature regression, which bears on the sample-size version of double descent. It does not reproduce the original model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.gate_note: The introduction cites prior work on double descent as a phenomenon random-feature models can capture; those cited results are not recorded. The study's own plots vary aspect ratio by subsampling training data and show test-risk curves. The supplied figure content does not permit reading their values or determining whether any peak occurs near the interpolation threshold.
record.test_reason: The paper derives and validates deterministic equivalents for test error of augmented random-feature ridge regression. Double descent appears only as a cited phenomenon in the introduction (Mei and Montanari 2022). The aspect-ratio curves (Figs 2, 4, 5) vary n by subsampling at fixed ridge (λ=0.05 or 1e-3). They are used to check theory-vs-empirics agreement and augmentation's bias/variance effect, not to test whether more data hurts near interpolation. The plotted values are unreadable in the supplied text. The authors draw no conclusion about non-monotonic sample-wise risk beyond mentioning 'the peak of the error curves' in the feature-map setting. The study therefore does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The paper derives non-asymptotic deterministic equivalents for the test error of augmented random-feature ridge regression, validates them on synthetic and MNIST data, and finds that augmentation improves generalization mainly via variance reduction under misspecification. It draws no conclusion about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: Studies augmented ridge/random-feature regression and varies the sample-to-feature aspect ratio; it does not use the original double-descent model-size or epoch-sweep procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The figures vary augmentation strength α and augmentation scheme; MNIST also compares identity and nontrivial feature maps. The supplied figure values are not readable.

fits_no_version.finding: Under feature misspecification, data augmentation lowers test error mainly by reducing variance, with little bias increase, across λ and aspect ratios.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data augmentation in misspecified random-feature regression acts mainly as variance reduction without a bias-variance trade-off.

record.problems: The figure content is garbled in the supplied text, preventing recovery of test-risk values, curve direction, or peak location. The reported experiments focus on augmentation and deterministic-equivalent accuracy rather than a direct double-descent test.
record.rows_left_out: No test-risk curves identified in the text were omitted. Bias and variance curves were left out because they are not test-error results for the claim versions.

untested.parts: Whether increasing n raises test error near p/n≈1. The curves exist but are neither analysed for this nor readable.
Whether ridge or augmentation strength removes a sample-wise peak. α and λ are varied, but peak behaviour is not reported.

missing.what: Authors note a peak in the test-error curves vs aspect ratio in the feature-map MNIST setting, where the theory fit is worst. The peak's location and height are not given. Kept so that the figure can be re-extracted if readable.

record.verdict_notes: The reader marked V3 as tested, but the study neither analyses nor reports sample-wise non-monotonicity, and all values are figure-only and garbled. Rows were relinked to none. If the figures become readable, the Fig 4/5 curves at small ridge (λ=1e-3, p=759) might show a peak near p/n≈1 and could then be re-evaluated for V3.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep and peak near the size that just fits the training set.
The plots vary training-set size through aspect ratio, but the supplied figure content does not establish whether increasing sample count raises test error near the interpolation threshold.
Capacity sweeps across model classes and behavior past the interpolation point.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across axes.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether peaks split, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
Whether counting effective parameters turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
